newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptians vote in low-key local elections.
newsitem.headline: Egyptians vote in low-key local elections.

text.p: Egyptians voted on Monday in local elections in which a low turnout of opposition candidates and fears of vote rigging look set to guarantee a sweeping victory for the ruling National Democratic Party (NDP).

Unlike the last local elections in 1992, Islamists present little if any threat to the government as police have been arresting candidates who openly espouse the politics of the Moslem Brotherhood -- Egypt's largest political Islamic group.

According to government figures released last week the NDP had won at least 50 percent of the 47,382 municipal council seats without a vote being cast because there were not enough opposition or independent candidates contesting them.

The independent Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights (EOHR) said in a statement on Monday the government had deprived thousands of people of their right to vote and run for the elections by barring many from electoral lists and creating administrative obstacles ahead of registration.
It said local officials had pressured independent candidates to withdraw to clear the way for NDP candidates.

Minister of Local Government Mahmoud Sherif told reporters there were less than 57,000 candidates. He said the violence in many constituencies during 1995 parliamentary elections put off many people from running in the municipal vote.

"Not enough candidates came forward to create competition in all councils. Some parties withdrew from the election because of the violence that we now know occurred during parliamentary elections and because of the astronomical sums spent on the campaign," Sherif said.
But Hassan Youssef, a lawyer with EOHR, said parties had either withdrawn or fielded a small number of candidates because they had lost faith in the election process.
"As usual they have little trust in the fairness or impartiality of the election process and because of the government's interference in the voting," he told Reuters.
The large Wafd party withdrew from the elections several weeks ago, citing its displeasure with the way they were conducted and expressing doubts that the vote would be fair.
Other parties such as the Ahrar and Nasserite parties have fielded a small number of candidates.

Police arrested 27 people including five journalists and a lawyer on Friday on suspicion of belonging to the outlawed and influential Moslem Brotherhood and using the election to spread the group's ideology.

EOHR said police in December arrested 40 members of the Labour opposition party on suspicion of belonging to the Brotherhood. Egyptian law bars anyone from carrying out any activity in the name of the Brotherhood.
The Egyptian government says the Brotherhood is a front for violent Moslem militant groups which are trying to turn Egypt into a strict Islamic state.
The Brotherhood denies the charge, saying it wants to use legal methods, such as elections, to bring about its version of an Islamic state.
In theory, Egypt is a multi-party democracy but in practice the NDP has held power unchallenged since former president Anwar Sadat created it in 1977.
One of the first voters on Monday was President Hosni Mubarak. He cast his ballot amid tight security at a school in the Cairo suburb of Heliopolis.
